Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules-2002
 
            
The Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 framed under the Securitisation & Reconstruction of Financial Assets &
Enforcement of Security Interest Ordinance, 2002 were examined and a questionnaire was forwarded to the Ministry of Finance (Banking
Division) on the 24 th November, 2003, to which the Ministry replied on the 7 th May, 2004. The Committee considered the Ministry’s
reply at its meeting held on 17 th November, 2005 and decided to seek further clarification on point No.1 (Rule 2 (d) defining ‘Approved
Valuer’). The Ministry vide their communication dated 29th November, 2006 provided the requisite clarification and also gave details of
the changes carried out by the Ministry on the other points on Committee’s suggestion.
 
2.         The points referred to the Ministry, their comments/clarifications and their Action Taken on each point are reproduced below: -
 
1.         Point raised- Rule 2(d) -
“Approved valuer” means a valuer as approved by the Board of Directors or Board of Trustees of the secured creditor, as the case
may be.
Should the approved valuer not be duly qualified; what is the justification for giving full discretion to the secured creditor in this
regard?
 
            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
Approved valuer means the professional who is qualified to value the property for a fee.  It is difficult to work out clear-cut
definition making exhaustive list of approved valuers in different fields and types of properties that are to be valued.   It is, however,
suggested that banks and financial institutions may be advised to utilize the services of valuers through Institution of Valuers who
claimed to be the only registered body in the country and their members are bound by code of conduct prescribed by it.  They are covered
by fee prescribed by the Government under Rule 8C of the Wealth Tax Act and also by CBDT.
 
Action Taken by the Ministry : (29.11.2006)
In terms of Rule 8(5) of Security Enforcement Rules, 2002, before effecting sale of immovable property, the authorized officer is
required to obtain valuation of the property from an approved valuer and in consultation with the secured creditor, fix the reserve price of
the property.  Chapter VII-B (Section 34 AB) of Wealth Tax Act, 1957 provides for registration of valuers.  Any person who possesses
the qualifications prescribed under Rule 8A of Wealth Tax Rules, 1957, may apply to the Chief Commissioner or Director General for
being registered as a valuer under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.  In terms of Rule 8A ibid, different qualifications have been prescribed for
valuers of different classes of assets (like for agricultural land, for plantations, for forests, for mines & quarries, for plant and machinery,
for immovable property other than agricultural land, plantations etc.).  We may not have objection in suitably modifying the definition of
Approved Valuer, “to mean a person registered as a valuer under Section 34 AB of Wealth Tax Act, 1957 and approved by the Board of
Directors or Board of Trustees of the secured creditor, as the case may be”.

2.         Point raised- Rule 4(1)
Where the possession of the secured assets to be taken by the secured creditor are movable property in possession of the borrower,
the authorized officer shall take possession of such movable property in the presence of two witnesses after a Panchanama drawn and
signed by the witnesses as nearly as possible in Appendix-I to these rules
Are these two witnesses, the witnesses, of the secured creditor or they are the public/independent witnesses; should the rule not
clarify on this point?
 
            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
Witnesses could be any one.  Flexibility in this matter is desirable and is recognized by the legislation as well as judiciary.   No
clarification in the Rule is necessary, as the present provision does not confine witnesses to specific classes of persons.
 
3.         Point raised- Rule 4(3)
The authorized officer shall keep the property taken possession under sub-rules (1) either in his own custody or in the custody of
any person authorized or appointed by him, who shall take as much care of the property in his custody as an owner of ordinary prudence
would, under the similar circumstances, take of such property.
                                   
 
This rule involves further delegation of power by the authorized officer to any person authorized or appointed by him without
fixing any responsibility either to the authorized officer or the person so authorized or appointed by him in case there is any damage to
the movable property in custody inadvertently.   Should the rule not vest ultimate responsibility on the authorised officer even in case
where he has authorized some body in this behalf?
 
Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
In terms of Rule 4(3), the Authorised Officer shall take as much care of the property in his custody as owner of ordinary
prudence.  Further as per Rule 4(4), the Authorised Officer shall take steps for preservation and protection of secured assets and insure
them, if necessary, till they are sold or otherwise disposed of.  Therefore even though the Authorised Officer is empowered to entrust the
possession to others; he is still responsible for acts of the custodian appointed by him to keep the assets.  Moreover, in terms of Section 19
of the Act, if the DRT or DRAT holds the possession of secured assets by the secured creditor as wrongful and directs the secured
creditor to return such assets to the borrower, such borrower shall be entitled to payment of such compensation and costs as may be
determined by the DRT or DRAT.  Hence, no specific provision, as contemplated by the Committee is necessary.
 
4.         Point raised- Rule 5
Valuation of movable secured assets: After taking possession under sub-rule (1) of the Rule 4 and in any case before
sale, the authorized officer shall obtain the estimated value of the movable secured assets and thereafter, if considered
necessary, fix in consultation with the secured creditor, the reserve price of the assets to be sold in realization of the dues of
the secured creditor.
While the rule envisages consultation with the secured creditor; why the borrower is not involved at all in fixing the reserve price
of the assets to be sold in realization of the dues of the secured creditor?
 
            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
In the light of the Supreme Court observations in Haryana Financial Corporation V.Jagadamba (2002) 110 Comp. Case 20 (SC),
notice of intended sale to the defaulting borrower is sufficient and any procedure requiring the defaulting borrower to be associated or
consulted in every stage in the sale of secured assets will place unnecessary restrictions in the exercise of the powers vested with the
secured creditors.  Further, in terms of Rule 6(1), the Authorised Officer is expected to secure the maximum sale price of the property to
be sold.
 
5.         Point raised- Rule 6(3)
Sale by any methods other than public auction or public tender, shall be on such terms as may be settled between the parties in
writing.
Shouldn’t the settlement between the parties before being finalized be conveyed to the borrower; Secondly should the terms
settled between the parties not be required to be kept open for the sake of transparency?
 
            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
As at 4 above.  To add, the Rules 6 and 9 provide for sufficient transparency of the transactions of sale.  The authorized officer is

public notice in Newspapers in case of public auction or invitation of tenders from public.   Further, borrower or secured creditor is not
prohibited from participation in the sale process, i.e. he can bid and purchase the secured assets.

10.       Point raised- Rule 8(6) proviso (c)
 Provided that if the sale of such secured assets is being effected by either inviting tenders from the public or by holding public
auction, the secured creditor shall cause a public note in two leading newspapers one in vernacular language having sufficient circulation

     (c) reserve price, below which the property may not be sold.
The word “may” should be replaced by the word “shall” to make the provisions certain that the property shall not be sold below
reserve price.
 
Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
In terms of second proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 9, if the Authorised office fails to obtain a price higher than the reserve price, he
may, with the consent of the borrower and the secured creditor effect the sale at such price.  Otherwise, by virtue of first proviso to sub-
Rule (2) of Rule 9, no sale of immovable property shall be confirmed, if the amount offered by sale price is less than the reserve price.  
The exception to sale below the reserve price with the consent of the secured creditor as well as borrower is to meet the situation when
the property is not likely to fetch the price reserved in view of the market condition.  The purpose behind having the word “may” is that it
would enable the secured creditor to sell the property and realize the dues.  It would not be possible if the word “shall” were used.  Using
the word “shall” will mean that property shall not be sold below the reserve price.   As regards any protection for such sales, it is held that
protection to secured creditor is the consent given by the borrower.  Hence, the use of the word ‘may’ in the Rule is apt.

 Time of sale, Issue of sale certificate and delivery of possession, etc. – (1) No sale, of immovable property under

            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
The sale of immovable property can take place only after the process of serving/publication of notice is completed.   Hence, the

The balance amount of purchase price payable shall be paid by the purchaser to the authorized officer on or before

            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
This is a discretion provided to the secured creditor to accept payment for sale of immovable property even after the statutory

contingencies of further cost, expenses and interest without any approval or control of either the Board of Directors of the secured

            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
(a ) The person, who purchases the property, takes it subject to the subsequent encumbrances, if any, it possess, with the full
knowledge thereof.  Hence, if he desires to have the property free of encumbrance, he shall take steps to get the encumbrance discharged. 
This is, therefore, an enabling provision.  Also, it may be noted that in terms of sub-Rules (8) to (10), the authorized officer, who received
the payment to the party entitled to the payment pursuant to release of encumbrance, deliver property free of encumbrance (known to the
secured creditor) to the purchaser and issue sale certificate indicating the sale free of any encumbrance known to the secured.  Thus, it is
the choice of the purchase to purchase the property subject to encumbrance or free of encumbrance.
(b ) The suggestion of the Committee can be considered i.e. to provide for approval of the secured creditor as to the
additional amount required from the purchaser to discharge the subsequent encumbrance.
 
Action Taken by the Ministry : (29.11.2006)
The authorized officer is a responsible officer who will discharge his functions strictly in accordance with law.  When a property
is sold subject to any encumbrances, there may be some expenditure to discharge the encumbrances and to meet contingencies of further
costs.  The authorized officer must have the discretion to determine the amount.   To make such determination subject to the approval of
the Board of Directors or the Board of Trustees would only mean further delay and adding another layer of decision making to what is a
normal administrative matter.  Government is of the view that there is no need to add a layer of approval by the Board of Directors or the
Board of Trustees in order to check possible misuse.  If, in any case, misuse is brought to the notice of the Board of Directors or the
Board of Trustees, they could always revise the order of the authorized officer or take suitable action against him.  We should not add
more and more layers to decision making in what are purely administrative matters.   The only safeguard that we may add to Rule 9(7) is
making a proviso that if any money remains unspent out of the deposit made by the purchaser, after meeting the cost of removing
encumbrances and contingencies, that amount shall be returned to the purchaser.  It is therefore, suggested that following proviso may be
added below sub-rule (7) of Rule 9.
“Provided that if after meeting the cost of removing encumbrances and contingencies there is any surplus available out of the
money deposited by the purchaser such surplus shall be paid to the purchaser within 15 days from the date of finalisation of the sale”

The Manager appointed by the Board of Directors or Board of Trustees, as the case may be, shall be deemed to be an

            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
Although the Manager is appointed by the secured creditor to manage these secured assets, the possession of which is already
taken by the secured creditor, the secured creditor continues to be the mortgage only and the ownership remains with the borrower.  
However, since the control over the property passes with the possession to the secured creditor for realization of dues, very little control
remains with the borrower to deal with the property.  Hence, there is a merit in the suggestion of the Committee, particularly when only
consultation and not approval of the borrower is required for appointment of a manager.  Hence, the provision need reconsideration.
           
Action Taken by the Ministry : (29.11.2006)
The Rules as it stands, carves out an exception where any acts of omission or commission are due to the improper intervention of
the secured creditor or the authorized officer and in such a case the borrower is not responsible.  The provisions contained in sub rule (2)
of rule 10 are on the lines of the provisions contained in sub section (3) of section 69A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.  The said

provision.

Delhi Advocates' Welfare Fund Rules, 2001.
 
            The Delhi Advocates' Welfare Fund Rules, 2001 framed under the Advocates' Welfare Fund Act, 2001 were examined
and a questionnaire on the subject was forwarded to the Ministry of Law & Justice (Department of Legal Affairs) on the 17 th
January, 2003 for furnishing their comments. The Ministry vide  their communication dated the 12 th May, 2005 furnished their
comments.
 
            The Committee considered the subject matter at its meeting held on 24th October, 2005. The points raised and Ministry's
comments are as follows: -
 
1)         Point referred (Rule 9(8) )-
 
"The Chairperson or the person presiding over a meeting shall have and exercise a second or a casting vote in all cases of
equality of votes."
Would it not be more appropriate if the Chairman does not exercise voting right in the normal course but votes only to
remove the tie?
            Ministry's Comments (12.05.05):-
The suggestion that the Chairman, who exercises the voting right only to remove the tie, is appreciated. The casting vote
in all cases of equality appears to be vague.
2)         Point referred (Rule 9(12) )-
 
"Meeting of the Trustee Committee shall, ordinarily, be held at its Office."
 
            The word 'ordinarily' used in the Regulation appears to be vague. Under what circumstances, meeting of the Committee
may be held at the places other than its office?        
Ministry's Comments (12.05.05):-
            The Rule as it exists appears to be in order. Of course, it impliedly gives the power to hold the meeting at any other place
other than its office if it is not ordinarily possible to hold the meeting at its office.
 
3)         Point referred (Rule 12(1) )-
 
"The Bar Council of Delhi may issue a certificate of recognition in Form IV, after such enquiry as it deems necessary, on
the application, made under Rule II."
            Rule 12(2
)- "The Bar Council of Delhi may recognize more than one association of advocates functioning at a particular
court, tribunal or other authority."
            Rule 12(3
)- "The Bar Council of Delhi shall prepare list of recognized association of advocates and update the same
from time to time."
 
(a)        Whether the Ministry have any objection in prescribing a specific time period within which certificate for recognition
may be issued to the association of advocates.
(b)        There is no provision in the rule for appeal/review if the application for recognition is rejected. The Ministry may please
comment.
            Ministry's Comments (12.05.05):-
(a) A period of four months initially may be prescribed for issuing a certificate for recognition.
(b) It would be appropriate if appeal can be prescribed, for which adjudicating authority may be the State Bar Council of
each State.
 
 
4)         Point referred (Rule 13(2))-
 
 "An advocate having membership in more than one association of advocates shall so apply from any one of them."
Why Rule 13(2) contemplates membership of more than one association of advocates, when an advocate can apply only
through one association? Should the rules not prohibit membership of more than one association by an advocate?
            Ministry's Comments (12.05.05):-
            The Rule appears to be clear that an advocate can apply from any one of the associations. The Rule appears to be
reasonable and requires no change.

Ministry’s reply
            The Regulations have been laid on the table of both the Houses of Parliament.   They were laid in the Rajya Sabha on
14.12.1994 and in the Lok Sabha on 19.12.1994.

            The Committee pointed out the considerable delay on the part of the Ministry in framing of Regulations which could

            “These regulations may be called “The Transport, Handling and Storage of Dangerous Goods in Bombay Port
Regulations, 1994” and are framed under the provisions of clauses (f) and (n) of section 123 of Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 (38
of 1963) made by the Port of Bombay”.
The date of commencement of these regulations has not been indicated which is an essential component of any
rule/regulation.  The Ministry may please indicate the date of commencement of these regulations in the regulations itself.
Ministry’s reply

Point-3: Regulation 4.4 (iii) – Dangerous Goods
            “Dangerous Goods mean goods which by reason of the nature, quantity or mode of storage of such goods are either
singly or collectively liable to endanger the life or the health of the persons within the port limits or on a vessel or to cause
damage to property within such port limits and includes such goods contained in a receptacle, portable tank, freight container or
vehicle as defined in the IMDG Code.  The term includes an empty receptacle, portable tank or tank vehicle which as been
previously used for carriage of dangerous goods unless such receptacle has been cleaned and dried or when the nature of the
former contents permits such carriage with safety and allow the containers to be closed securely.
Dangerous goods include all substance
(i)
                  Having properties coming within the classes listed in the IMDG Code;
(ii)                Substance defined as explosive as defined by the Explosive e Act, 1884 and /or the Explosive Rules, 1983;
(iii)               Any other goods which the competent authority may specify as dangerous goods;
(iv)              Hazardous chemicals listed in Schedule-1 of the Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules,
1989”.
The regulation gives discretionary powers to the competent authority to specify and good as dangerous one.  Whether
such powers are exercised judiciously and are not liable to be misused?
Ministry’s reply
            Classification of the dangerous goods is based on International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code (IMDG Code). 
However, new types of hazardous chemicals are being manufactured, transported and traded.   Thus, Port may be called upon to
handle new chemicals before they are classified and listed under IMDG Code.  Hence, the Port has been vested with
discretionary powers to handle such chemicals.  However, these powers are exercised judiciously as the decision is based on the
chemical composition details of such goods obtained from the manufacturers and the importers/exporters.   Under the
circumstances Competent Authority has been assigned some discretionary powers.
Committee’s observation
The Committee noted the explanation given by the Ministry.
 
Point-4:Regulation 4.8 – Inspector of dangerous goods.
            “Inspector of Dangerous goods for the purpose of the regulations means a person appointed by the Competent Authority
to ensure compliance with these rules at any handling, storage, disposal or transport of the dangerous goods coming to this port”
            Should any technical/professional qualification/practical experience not be prescribed for the person to be appointed as
Inspector of Dangerous Goods?
Ministry’s reply
            The Asstt. Manager (Hazardous Cargo) has been appointed as the Inspector of Dangerous Goods under these regulations
and he is responsible for carrying out the responsibilities under these regulations.  For appointment to this post, the requirements
are laid down and include minimum post graduate qualification in Chemistry and experience of 5 years in handling, stowage and
storage of dangerous and hazardous chemicals in a factory or a manufacturing industry.  Besides, the incumbent is also given
training from time to time to keep pace with the new developments with regard to dangerous cargo, their safe storage and
transportation, etc.
Committee’s observation
            The Committee desired that the technical/professional qualifications/practical experience prescribed for appointment of
Inspector of dangerous goods should be indicated in the regulations itself.

            “Responsible Person – Responsible person means a person appointed by the Owner and/or Master and empowered to
